pg_21__page_5_Figure_12.jpeg.description:
A two-dimensional Cartesian coordinate plane representing commodity space, labeled 'Figure 1.1'. The horizontal axis is labeled $x_1$ (representing the quantity of gadgets) and the vertical axis is labeled $x_2$ (representing the quantity of widgets). Two distinct points (commodity bundles) are plotted as solid black dots on the plane:
1. A point labeled $(2, 6)$ in the upper-left region, with dashed reference lines extending vertically to the horizontal axis at $x_1 = 2$ and horizontally to the vertical axis at $x_2 = 6$.
2. A point labeled $(5, 3)$ in the lower-right region, with dashed reference lines extending vertically to the horizontal axis at $x_1 = 5$ and horizontally to the vertical axis at $x_2 = 3$.

pg_21__page_6_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A graph titled Figure 1.2 showing indifference curves in a two-dimensional commodity space. The vertical axis is labeled 'W' and the horizontal axis is labeled 'G'. Three convex, downward-sloping curves represent different levels of utility: the innermost curve is labeled 'u = 1', the middle curve is labeled 'u = 6', and the outermost curve is labeled 'u = 10'. An arrow points outward from the 'u = 1' curve toward the higher utility curves, indicating increasing utility as one moves away from the origin.

pg_21__page_7_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional economic graph illustrating a consumer's budget constraint and indifference curves. The vertical axis represents one good (with intercept labeled D), the horizontal axis represents another good (with intercept labeled A), and the origin is labeled 0. A straight line connects D on the vertical axis to A on the horizontal axis, forming a shaded triangular budget set beneath it. Three downward-sloping, convex indifference curves are shown; the middle curve, labeled 'u', is tangent to the budget line segment DA at a point labeled 'c'. This point 'c' represents the utility-maximizing consumption bundle subject to the budget constraint.

pg_21__page_8_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional microeconomic graph illustrating budget constraints and indifference curves. The vertical axis starts at origin O, and the horizontal axis represents quantities of a commodity. Two budget lines are shown: line DA connecting point D on the vertical axis to point A on the horizontal axis, and line D'A' connecting point D' to point A', situated further out from the origin. Three downward-sloping, convex indifference curves are depicted. Budget line DA is tangent to an indifference curve at point C. Budget line D'A' is tangent to a higher indifference curve at point C', showing a shift to a higher level of utility as the budget constraint expands.

pg_21__page_8_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A microeconomics graph illustrating indifference curves and budget lines for consumer choice. The vertical axis starts at origin 0 and has an intercept labeled D. Two downward-sloping, convex indifference curves are shown. From point D on the vertical axis, two budget lines extend downward to the horizontal axis: line DA ends at point A on the horizontal axis, and line DA' ends at point A' on the horizontal axis closer to the origin. Budget line DA is tangent to the higher indifference curve at point C. Budget line DA' is tangent to the lower indifference curve at point C'.

pg_21__page_11_Figure_197.jpeg.description: A horizontal number line representing the real numbers (R^1). It extends endlessly in both directions, indicated by arrows at both ends. Centered at 0, the line includes marked integers ranging from -6 to 6, with negative numbers labeled to the left of 0 and positive numbers labeled to the right.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_11.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph showing a straight line with a positive slope. The line passes through the y-axis at approximately (0, 1) and through the x-axis at approximately (-1, 0), extending infinitely in both directions across the four quadrants.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_12.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate plane showing a continuous line passing through the origin (0,0). For x < 0, the line has a steeper slope, rising quickly as it approaches zero from the left. For x >= 0, the line continues into the first quadrant with a slightly less steep slope, illustrating a piecewise linear continuous function that is strictly increasing everywhere.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A graph of a parabola opening upwards with its vertex at the origin (0, 0) on a Cartesian coordinate plane. The curve is symmetric about the y-axis, located entirely in the first and second quadrants where y is greater than or equal to 0.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_14.jpeg.description: A plot of a strictly decreasing function $f(x)$ on a Cartesian coordinate plane. The curve descends from the upper-left quadrant, flattens horizontally at its inflection point where it crosses the origin $(0,0)$ with a derivative equal to zero ($f'(0) = 0$), and then continues downwards into the lower-right quadrant. This illustrates a function that is strictly decreasing throughout its domain even though its derivative is zero at a single point.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_15.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a downward-opening parabola with its vertex centered at the origin (0, 0). The curve is symmetric across the vertical y-axis and extends downwards into the third and fourth quadrants.

pg_21__page_13_Figure_17.jpeg.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane showing a graph of a smooth, U-shaped convex curve (parabola-like function f). The curve reaches its lowest point, marked with a solid black dot, at x-coordinate x_0 and y-coordinate f(x_0). Dashed lines project from the minimum point to the y-axis at f(x_0) and down toward x_0 on the x-axis, illustrating the local/global minimum of the function.

pg_21__page_14_Figure_2.jpeg.description: A plot showing a continuous curve $g(z)$ opening downward (concave down) on a Cartesian coordinate system. The vertex of the curve is at a maximum point marked with a solid dot at coordinates $(z_0, g(z_0))$. Dashed projection lines extend from the vertex down to $z_0$ on the horizontal axis and left to $g(z_0)$ on the vertical axis.

pg_21__page_17_Figure_11.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating three straight lines labeled l_1, l_2, and l_3 to demonstrate the concept of line slopes.

- Line l_1 is a steep line sloping upward from left to right. It passes through the marked points (1, 0) and (2, 3). Annotations show a horizontal change (run) of 1 unit between x = 1 and x = 2, and a vertical change (rise) of 3 units between y = 0 and y = 3, illustrating a slope of 3.
- Line l_2 is a line sloping upward at a 45-degree angle, representing a slope of +1.
- Line l_3 is a line sloping downward from left to right at a -45-degree angle, representing a slope of -1.

pg_21__page_18_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the slope of a line passing through four distinct points across different quadrants. The line passes through points marked (x_1, y_1), (x_1 + 1, y_1'), (x_2, y_2), (x_2 + 1, y_2'), (x_3, y_3), and (x_4, y_4). Three right-angled triangles labeled #1, #2, and #3 are constructed along the line to demonstrate slope equality using similar triangles. Triangle #1 has a horizontal base of length 1 and a vertical height of y_1' - y_1. Triangle #2 has a horizontal base of length 1 and a vertical height of y_2' - y_2. Triangle #3, located in the first quadrant between (x_3, y_3) and (x_4, y_4), has a horizontal base of length x_4 - x_3 and a vertical height of y_4 - y_3.

pg_21__page_21_Figure_89.jpeg.description:
Figure 2.7 shows four lines labeled (a), (b), (c), and (d) in the plane:
- Line (a) slopes upwards from left to right at a moderate positive slope.
- Line (b) slopes downwards from left to right at a negative slope.
- Line (c) is a horizontal line with a slope of zero.
- Line (d) is a steeply rising line sloping upwards from left to right with a large positive slope.

pg_21__page_22_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A graph of a smooth, wave-like function $f(x)$ plotted on a Cartesian coordinate system with $x$ and $y$ axes. On the upper-left curve of the function, a specific point is marked with a black dot corresponding to the horizontal coordinate $x_0$ and vertical value $f(x_0)$. A straight line tangent to the curve is drawn through this point, illustrating the geometric concept of the derivative (slope of the tangent line) at $x_0$.

pg_21__page_23_Figure_177.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating the concepts of tangent and non-tangent lines on the cubic curve y = x^3. The coordinate axes intersect at the origin (0,0). The curve y = x^3 passes through the origin, where the x-axis acts as a tangent line that crosses through the curve. Point A lies in the first quadrant on the curve, where a non-tangent line with a negative slope intersects the curve at point A and passes through it.

pg_21__page_24_Figure_13.jpeg.description: A graph illustrating secant lines converging toward a tangent line on a curve f(x). The horizontal axis shows x-values labeled x_0, x_0 + h_3, x_0 + h_2, and x_0 + h_1 from left to right. A smooth, downward-concave curve passes through the base point (x_0, f(x_0)) and three points to its right: (x_0 + h_3, f(x_0 + h_3)), (x_0 + h_2, f(x_0 + h_2)), and (x_0 + h_1, f(x_0 + h_1)). Three secant lines, labeled \ell_3, \ell_2, and \ell_1, each pass through (x_0, f(x_0)) and one of the respective points on the curve. As the step size h_n decreases from h_1 to h_3, the secant lines become progressively steeper, approaching the tangent line at (x_0, f(x_0)).

pg_21__page_25_Figure_103.jpeg.description: A Cartesian plot showing a parabola given by $f(x) = x^2$ with its vertex at the origin $(0,0)$. On the right branch of the parabola, a point is plotted at $(3,9)$. A straight tangent line is drawn passing through the point $(3,9)$ and touching the parabola at that location.

pg_21__page_30_Figure_93.jpeg.description: A graph of the absolute value function, y = |x|, plotted on Cartesian coordinates with horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis. The graph forms a V-shape symmetric about the y-axis, with its vertex at the origin (0,0), demonstrating a sharp corner or non-smooth point where the derivative does not exist.

pg_21__page_30_Figure_101.jpeg.description: A geometric plot on a Cartesian coordinate plane illustrating the graph of the absolute value function, $y = |x|$, along with several secant lines passing through the origin $(0,0)$. The V-shaped graph of $|x|$ opens upwards from the origin into the upper two quadrants. Three distinct lines, labeled $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_3$, pass through the origin at varying slopes. Line $\ell_1$ has a small positive slope, line $\ell_2$ has a smaller negative slope closer to horizontal, and line $\ell_3$ has a steeper negative slope. Each line extends into both opposite quadrants across the origin, demonstrating different secant lines approaching the origin from different directions.

pg_21__page_31_Figure_132.jpeg.description: A graph of a piecewise function g showing a discontinuity at x = 0. For x < 0, the curve decreases smoothly toward a lower point on the y-axis (leaving an open gap/end at x = 0 below the x-axis). For x >= 0, there is a solid black dot above the x-axis on the y-axis, from which a straight line extends upward and to the right into the first quadrant.

pg_21__page_37_Figure_8.jpeg.description:
A mathematical graph illustrating differential approximation on a coordinate system with axes labeled x and an unlabeled vertical axis (y-axis). A curve representing a function f(x) and its tangent line at a point x_0 are shown.

Key elements:
- On the horizontal x-axis, two points are marked: x_0 and x_0 + \Delta x.
- On the vertical axis, three y-values are marked with dashed horizontal projection lines:
  - f(x_0) corresponding to x_0 on the curve.
  - f(x_0 + \Delta x) corresponding to x_0 + \Delta x on the curve.
  - f(x_0) + f'(x_0) \Delta x corresponding to x_0 + \Delta x on the tangent line.
- Points marked on the plot:
  - A black dot at (x_0, f(x_0)) where the tangent line touches the curve f(x).
  - A black dot on the curve at x_0 + \Delta x, corresponding to height f(x_0 + \Delta x).
  - A black dot on the tangent line at x_0 + \Delta x, corresponding to height f(x_0) + f'(x_0) \Delta x.
- Vertical increments:
  - \Delta y = f(x_0 + \Delta x) - f(x_0) is shown with a brace indicating the change in the actual function's y-value from x_0 to x_0 + \Delta x.
  - dy = f'(x_0) \Delta x is shown with a brace indicating the vertical change along the tangent line from x_0 to x_0 + \Delta x.

pg_21__page_40_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph displaying an exponential growth curve y = b^x (where b > 1). The graph shows an increasing function passing through the y-intercept at (0, 1), marked with a solid dot. Additional solid dots are plotted along the curve at both negative and positive x-values, demonstrating how the curve approaches the horizontal x-axis asymptotically to the left and rises steeply to the right.

pg_21__page_41_Figure_0.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating three exponential functions: y = 10^x (represented by a long-dashed line), y = 3^x (represented by a dotted line), and y = 2^x (represented by a solid line). All three curves pass through the common y-intercept point at (0, 1). For x > 0, the curve y = 10^x rises the steepest, followed by y = 3^x, and then y = 2^x. For x < 0, all three curves approach the horizontal asymptote y = 0 as x goes to negative infinity, with y = 10^x closest to the x-axis.

pg_21__page_41_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A plot showing the graph of the exponential function y = (1/2)^x. The vertical y-axis and horizontal x-axis intersect at the origin (0,0). The curve drops steeply from the upper-left quadrant, passing through marked points at x = -3 (y = 8), x = -2 (y = 4), x = -1 (y = 2), the y-intercept at (0, 1), and continues through x = 1 (y = 1/2), x = 2 (y = 1/4), and x = 3 (y = 1/8), approaching the positive x-axis as a horizontal asymptote.

pg_21__page_46_Figure_151.jpeg.description:
A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating the inverse relationship between the exponential function y = 10^x and the logarithmic function y = Log x. The graph shows three curves/lines:
1. The curve y = 10^x in the upper-left to upper-right area, passing through the y-intercept dot at (0, 1) and approaching the negative x-axis asymptotically.
2. The diagonal line y = x passing through the origin (0, 0), acting as the axis of symmetry.
3. The curve y = Log x in the lower-left to lower-right area, passing through the x-intercept dot at (1, 0) and approaching the negative y-axis asymptotically. The graph visually shows that y = Log x is the reflection of y = 10^x across the line y = x.

pg_21__page_54_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate graph showing a bell-shaped curve representing a standard normal-like exponential function, specifically $y = e^{-x^2/2}$. The horizontal x-axis has tick marks with labeled points at -1, 0, and 1. The vertical y-axis is labeled with values around 0.6 and 1. Three prominent solid black dots mark key coordinates on the curve: the peak at $(0, 1)$, and two inflection points symmetric about the y-axis at $(-1, e^{-1/2} \approx 0.6)$ and $(1, e^{-1/2} \approx 0.6)$. The curve smoothly approaches the x-axis asymptotically as $x$ goes to positive or negative infinity.

pg_171__page_5_Figure_7.jpeg.description: A portion of a horizontal real number line (Figure 10.1) displaying integer values marked from -6 on the left to 6 on the right, centered around 0.

pg_171__page_6_Figure_146.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate system diagram demonstrating how a point in the plane is identified by an ordered pair (a, b). The origin (0, 0) is at the intersection of the horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis, with tick marks indicating integer values -1, 0, 1, 2, and 3 along the x-axis, and -1 and 1 along the y-axis. A vertical dashed line labeled l_1 passes through x = a on the x-axis, where a is approximately -2.5. A horizontal dashed line labeled l_2 passes through y = b on the y-axis, where b is approximately 2.5. The point of intersection of lines l_1 and l_2 in the upper-left quadrant (Quadrant II) is plotted with a solid black dot and labeled with the ordered pair (a, b).

pg_171__page_6_Figure_152.jpeg.description:
A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane plot showing four plotted points with dashed grid projection lines. The horizontal axis ranges from -4 to 4, and the vertical axis ranges from -3 to 3, intersecting at the origin (0, 0).

The four plotted points are:
1. Top-left quadrant (Quadrant II): Point labeled (-2, 2) located at x = -2, y = 2.
2. Bottom-left quadrant (Quadrant III): Point labeled (-2, -1) located at x = -2, y = -1.
3. Top-right quadrant (Quadrant I): Point labeled (3, 2) located at x = 3, y = 2.
4. Bottom-right quadrant (Quadrant IV): Point labeled (3, -1) located at x = 3, y = -1.

pg_171__page_7_Figure_5.jpeg.description: A 3D Cartesian coordinate system with three axes labeled x_1, x_2, and x_3. The x_2 axis is drawn horizontally, with x_2 extending to the right and left with regularly spaced tick marks. The x_3 axis is drawn vertically, with positive x_3 extending upward and negative x_3 extending downward, marked with tick marks and a highlighted thick vertical segment along the positive x_3 axis. The x_1 axis extends forward and down-left (drawn as a solid line in the third quadrant) and is extended backward into the upper-right quadrant as a dashed line. The axes intersect at the origin (0, 0, 0).

pg_171__page_7_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A 3D Cartesian coordinate system with axes labeled x_1, x_2, and x_3. The diagram illustrates how a point in 3D space is located by moving along each coordinate direction. Eight vertices of a rectangular prism (cuboid) are marked with black dots and labeled with their coordinates: (0,0,c), (0,b,c), (0,b,0), (a,0,c), (a,b,c), (a,0,0), and (a,b,0). Line segments representing lengths along or parallel to the axes are labeled 'a' (parallel to the x_1-axis), 'b' (parallel to the x_3-axis), and 'c' (parallel to the x_2-axis), showing the vector displacement components from the origin or projections onto planes.

pg_171__page_9_Figure_2.jpeg.description: Figure 10.6 illustrates multiple identical displacement vectors on a Cartesian coordinate plane. Four parallel arrows of equal length and direction point up and to the right, each representing the vector displacement (3, 2). One vector starts at the origin (0, 0) and ends at (3, 2). A second vector starts at point P and ends at point Q, labeled as vector v. Two other vectors are shown starting at different initial points in the second and third quadrants, demonstrating that the same displacement vector can be applied at various initial positions across the plane.

pg_171__page_10_Figure_1.jpeg.description:
A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane showing five vectors originating from the origin (0,0):
1. A vector pointing to (-4, -2) in the third quadrant.
2. A vector pointing to (-2, 2) in the second quadrant.
3. A vector pointing to (1, 3) in the first quadrant.
4. A vector pointing to (2, 1) in the first quadrant.
5. A vector pointing along the positive x-axis to (4, 0).

pg_171__page_11_Figure_10.jpeg.description: A geometric vector diagram in a 2D Cartesian coordinate system showing vector addition u + v. The origin (0,0) serves as the starting point. Vector u extends from the origin to point (a, b), marked with label 'u'. Vector v is shown starting at the origin going to (c, d), and also translated so its tail is at the head of u, ending at (a + c, b + d). The resultant vector u + v is drawn as a diagonal vector starting from the origin directly to the point (a + c, b + d). The x-axis shows marked ticks at c, a, and a + c. The y-axis shows marked ticks at d, b, and b + d.

pg_171__page_12_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A vector diagram illustrating the commutative law of vector addition, u + v = v + u, using a parallelogram. Originating from a common starting point at the bottom-left corner on a two-dimensional coordinate system, vector u forms the bottom side pointing right and slightly up, while vector v forms the left side pointing up and to the right. Following vector v with vector u (top side) leads to the same terminal point at the top-right corner as following vector u with vector v (right side). The diagonal vector stretching from the origin to the top-right corner is labeled as both u + v (above the diagonal) and v + u (below the diagonal).

pg_171__page_13_Figure_4.jpeg.description: A vector diagram in a 2D Cartesian coordinate plane showing vector subtraction as triangle completion. Vector y starts at the origin (0,0) and points up and to the right into the first quadrant. Vector x also starts at the origin (0,0) and extends further to the right with a gentler upward slope. The vector x - y starts at the terminal point (arrowhead) of vector y and extends down and to the right to meet the terminal point (arrowhead) of vector x, illustrating that y + (x - y) = x.

pg_171__page_14_Picture_13.jpeg.description:
A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane illustrating scalar multiplication of vectors. The origin is at the center with several vectors plotted in different quadrants:

1. In the first quadrant, vector x points up and right. In the third quadrant, its scalar multiple -2x points in the exact opposite direction and is twice as long.
2. In the first quadrant, a vector u points shallowly upwards and to the right, with a shorter vector marked as (1/2)u along the same ray.
3. In the second quadrant, vector w points up and left, and extending along the same direction to twice its length is vector 2w.
4. In the fourth quadrant, vector v points down and right, and extending along the same ray to four times its length is vector 4v.

pg_171__page_15_Diagram_1.jpeg.description:
A geometric vector diagram illustrating the associative property of vector addition: u + (v + w) = (u + v) + w. The diagram shows three consecutive directed vectors forming a polygon: vector u goes up and right from the origin; vector v continues nearly horizontally to the right from the tip of u; and vector w goes down and right from the tip of v to a final endpoint on the horizontal line.

Two intermediate diagonal vectors demonstrate the grouping of addition:
1. The vector labeled 'u + v' points directly from the origin to the tip of vector v.
2. The vector labeled 'v + w' points directly from the tip of vector u to the final endpoint (tip of vector w).

The resultant vector going straight along the bottom from the origin to the final endpoint represents both '(u + v) + w' and 'u + (v + w)', visually confirming that both groupings yield the exact same sum vector.

pg_171__page_16_Diagram_14.jpeg.description: A horizontal line segment lying at $y = b$ connects two points, $P(a_1, b)$ on the left and $Q(a_2, b)$ on the right. A vertical axis on the left indicates the $y$-value $b$ with a tick mark aligning with the horizontal segment.

pg_171__page_16_Diagram_15.jpeg.description: A horizontal number line intersected by a vertical axis at the origin (0). Two points are marked along the positive horizontal axis to the right of the vertical axis, labeled a1 and a2, with a1 located closer to the origin and a2 located further to the right.

pg_171__page_16_Diagram_18.jpeg.description: A Cartesian coordinate graph illustrating a vertical line segment connecting two points. The horizontal x-axis shows a mark at x = a. The vertical y-axis shows marks at y = b_1 and y = b_2. Point P is plotted at (a, b_1) and point Q is plotted at (a, b_2). A thick vertical line segment connects P and Q, representing the distance between two points that share the same x-coordinate.

pg_171__page_16_Diagram_21.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram on a Cartesian coordinate plane illustrating the distance between two points, P and Q. Point P is located at horizontal coordinate a_1 and vertical coordinate b_1. Point R is directly to the right of P at coordinate (a_2, b_1), forming a horizontal segment PR with length m. Point Q is directly above R at coordinate (a_2, b_2), forming a vertical segment QR with length n. The segment PQ is the hypotenuse of the right triangle PQR with length l, extending from P(a_1, b_1) to Q(a_2, b_2). The vertical axis on the left marks b_1 and b_2, and the horizontal axis below marks a_1 and a_2.

pg_171__page_17_Picture_9.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system diagram illustrating a geometric construction used to calculate distance in three dimensions using the Pythagorean theorem. The axes are labeled with ticks for $a_1, a_2$ along one inclined axis, $b_1, b_2$ along the horizontal axis, and $c_1, c_2$ along the vertical axis. A set of connected line segments forming right triangles connects points labeled $S$, $P$, $Q$, $R$, and $T$. Specifically, point $S$ lies at height $c_1$, line $SR$ is horizontal, line $QR$ is vertical, and right triangle right angles are marked at vertex $S$ and vertex $R$, illustrating orthogonal components for distance calculations.

pg_171__page_21_Picture_14.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system showing a plane embedded in space containing two vectors, u and v, originating from the same point at the origin. An arc indicates the angle theta (\theta) measured between the two vectors within the plane.

pg_171__page_21_Picture_20.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram showing an acute angle theta formed by vertex A, ray AC (the horizontal baseline), and line segment AB. Point D lies on the horizontal baseline line AC directly beneath point B, forming a right triangle BAD with angle theta at vertex A.

pg_171__page_21_Picture_23.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line passing through points D, A, and C from left to right. A vertical line segment BD extends upward from point D, forming a right triangle BDA. A line segment BA forms the hypotenuse. The angle supplementary to angle DAB, measured on the right side of line segment BA at point A relative to the horizontal line segment AC, is labeled with the Greek letter theta (θ). An arrow curved counterclockwise points to the segment BA.

pg_171__page_23_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A geometric vector diagram in a 2D coordinate system with origin 0. Vector u points from origin 0 to point P, forming an angle theta with vector v, which extends from origin 0 towards point Q. Point R lies on the line along vector v such that the line segment PR is perpendicular to vector v, indicated by a right-angle symbol at R. The vector from 0 to R is labeled tv, and the dashed vector from R to P is labeled u - tv. Line segment PR is also pointing to a label m.

pg_171__page_23_Picture_9.jpeg.description: A 3D Cartesian coordinate system diagram illustrating four vectors originating from the origin (0, 0, 0). Three basis vectors lie along the axes: vector u1 pointing to point (c, 0, 0) along the x-axis, vector u2 pointing to point (0, c, 0) along the y-axis, and vector u3 pointing to point (0, 0, c) along the z-axis. A space diagonal vector d points from the origin to the opposite corner of a cube at point (c, c, c). Dashed lines illustrate the cubic grid structure in three dimensions.

pg_171__page_24_Figure_9.jpeg.description: A geometric vector diagram showing vector addition using the triangle law on a two-dimensional coordinate system. A vector labelled 'u' extends pointing up and to the right from an initial point. From the terminal point of 'u', a second vector labelled 'v' extends pointing down and to the right. A third vector labelled 'u + v' goes directly from the initial point of 'u' to the terminal point of 'v', forming a triangle.

pg_171__page_27_Picture_13.jpeg.description: A geometric vector diagram showing a rhombus labeled with side vectors u and v. The bottom horizontal side is labeled vector 'u' and the left side pointing up and to the right is labeled vector 'v'. The top horizontal side is also labeled 'u' and the right side is labeled 'v'. The long diagonal connecting the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner represents the vector sum 'u + v'. The short diagonal connects the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner, intersecting the long diagonal.

pg_171__page_28_Picture_6.jpeg.description: A geometric diagram showing a parallelogram spanned by two vectors, u and v, originating from the same vertex at an angle theta (θ). Vector u points upward and to the right, forming the left side of the parallelogram. Vector v points to the right along the base. A dashed perpendicular height line, labeled h, drops from the tip of vector u to the base vector v.

pg_171__page_29_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate plane depicting two lines labeled 'a' and 'v'. Line 'a' is an inclined line passing through marked points (1, -1), (2, 0) on the x-axis, (4, 2), and (5, 3), with a y-intercept at (0, -2). Line 'v' is a vertical line located at x = 3.5 (passing through x = 3.5 on the horizontal axis).

pg_171__page_29_Figure_6.jpeg.description: A 2D coordinate system diagram showing the vector representation of a line. An initial position vector, labeled x_0, points from the origin to a point on the line. Starting from the head of x_0, a direction vector labeled v extends along the line. A point on the line farther along this direction is labeled with a solid dot and the expression x_0 + tv.

pg_171__page_32_Picture_11.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system showing a plane passing through the origin 0, defined by three axes x_1, x_2, and x_3. Two linearly independent vectors, labeled v and w, originate from the origin 0 and lie entirely within the plane, illustrating how two vectors span a plane through the origin.

pg_171__page_33_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system with axes x_1, x_2, and x_3 intersecting at the origin labeled 0. pg_171__page_34_Figure_1.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system with axes x1, x2, and x3 meeting at the origin O. pg_171__page_35_Picture_1.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system showing axes x1, x2, and x3 with origin 0. A plane is shown floating in 3D space. pg_171__page_38_Figure_165.jpeg.description: A two-dimensional coordinate plot showing a consumer's budget set in commodity space. pg_171__page_39_Figure_23.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system showing the standard 2-simplex (probability simplex for n = 3) in three-dimensional space. The vertices of the triangular surface are located at the points (1,0,0) on the x-axis, (0,1,0) on the y-axis, and (0,0,1) on the z-axis. pg_171__page_41_Figure_8.jpeg.description: A standard IS-LM model graph plotted on a two-dimensional Cartesian plane. The horizontal axis represents output/income, labeled 'Y', and the vertical axis represents the interest rate, labeled 'r'. A downward-sloping line labeled 'IS' intersects an upward-sloping line labeled 'LM'. Their point of intersection is marked with a filled black circle, which corresponds to the equilibrium output 'Y*' on the horizontal axis and the equilibrium interest rate 'r*' on the vertical axis.

pg_171__page_41_Figure_11.jpeg.description: An IS-LM graph showing the effect of an increase in government spending (G) or investment (I*). The vertical axis represents the interest rate (r) and the horizontal axis represents output/income (Y). An upward-sloping LM curve intersects two parallel, downward-sloping IS curves, labeled IS_0 and IS_1. pg_171__page_44_Figure_94.jpeg.description: A 2D Cartesian coordinate plot showing two axes labeled x1 (horizontal) and x2 (vertical). A line passing through the origin in the first and third quadrants is labeled L[v]. On this line, in the first quadrant, a bold arrow representing a vector originates from the origin and points along the line, labeled v. pg_171__page_44_Figure_102.jpeg.description: A 3D coordinate system graph with axes labeled $x_1$ (horizontal axis pointing right), $x_2$ (vertical axis pointing up), and $x_3$ (axis projecting forward-left).
